Size and shape affect the volume, timbre and resonance; the larger ones are louder, and players choose a size and a striking method to suit the venue, whether the performance is live or recorded, and whether there is amplification. By tapping lightly, striking the pair together, covering them with the hand or striking the rim, the player can produce a quiet click, a bell-like ring, a damped sound or a loud clash, with a small variation in pitch. Compared with clapper-type instruments such as spoons, bone plates and castanets, finger cymbals are fixed to the fingers and have a more metallic resonance.

They sound when two are struck together, and can make a light tap, a bell tone, a damped sound and a strong strike; a player who does not specialise in cymbals can also strike them with a drumstick, or pinch the strap between thumb and forefinger and knock the two rims together. A first rhythm can be the three-stroke figure left / right / left / rest, or four alternating strokes; after that come belly-dance rhythms such as beledi and chiftetelli, while in Sufi music they can be played as a long, unmeasured stream of sound.

They belong to the same family as the instruments used by Ottoman military bands, and are occasionally seen in Western orchestras and other music performance, usually for their bright sound with its Middle Eastern associations, mostly as rhythmic punctuation. Modern fusion music also uses finger cymbals, combining them with Arabic rhythms, jazz and electronic music.

Wooden krotala existed in ancient Greece by about 500 BCE, and pottery shows them being played at festivals; metal cymbals at that time were mostly struck one in each hand. Images of them tied to the fingers appear in the Roman Empire, and mosaics and reliefs in Bulgaria, Italy and Belgium date them to the second to fourth centuries. Whether the tradition was continuous afterwards is unclear, but clapper instruments carried on into the Middle Ages; the modern form of finger cymbals in Egypt and the Ottoman Empire is found by the eighteenth century at the latest. It became an important rhythmic element of Middle Eastern belly dance, Sufi music and zar ritual, and spread with regional styles and modern fusion music.

Finger cymbals are small metal cymbals of the Middle East, an idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 111.142. A set usually has four, two for each hand, tied to the thumb and middle finger with elastic cord or a leather strap; the player strikes two of them together, and they can also be struck with a drumstick, or held by their straps and knocked together. They belong to the clapper family and are common in belly dance, Sufi religious music, Egyptian zar healing rituals, and as punctuation in Ottoman military music and Western orchestras.
